source.title_on_document: Cross-lingual effects of AI-generated content on human work

supplement.holds: The main text refers to SI Section A for methods, B1.3 for task examples, B3.2 for rating dimensions, B3.1/B4.1 for evaluator demographics, and Fig. S1 for design (pp. 2-3). SI Tables S1-S2 concern model-output quality; S3-S4 participant descriptives and balance; S5 human email-quality regressions; S6 interrater agreement; S7-S8 prompt-length checks; S9 email length; S10 writing time; S11 confidence; S12 perceived difficulty; and S13 task-type heterogeneity (pp. 3-6). SI Figs. S2-S7 accompany the results. None of these tables or SI sections is included in this PDF. Exact coefficient tables, arm descriptive statistics, and any numerical standard errors must be checked in the supplement; their contents could not be verified. Main-text selected standardized differences and p-values are recorded below.

paper_design_summary: Study 1 asked trained evaluators to rate GPT-4 business recommendations produced in English, Arabic, and Chinese; it contains no human-created comparison output (p. 2, Methods). Study 2 randomly assigned a reported sample of 480 people to write a business email with supplied GPT-4 content or without AI content, and trained evaluators scored creativity, completeness, relevance, and actionability; email length was also measured (pp. 2-3, Methods and Statistical analysis; p. 6, Results). The assistance was pre-generated text displayed with the task, and the main results emphasize how the AI effect differs between language groups (pp. 2-3; p. 9, Limitations).

studies.label: Study 1: model-generated business recommendations across languages

assignment.what_was_assigned: No person was assigned to AI assistance: translated business prompts were submitted to GPT-4, and the generated outputs were evaluated across languages (p. 2, Methods).

participants.who: The corpus contains 600 AI-generated responses to 200 business prompts in three languages. Six native-speaking evaluators, two per language, had prior experience in relevant business domains and rated the responses; these evaluators are not people producing creative output under AI assistance (p. 2, Methods).
participants.quote: ChatGPT-4 was then used to generate responses to each prompt in all three languages, resulting in 600 AI-generated responses (200 prompts × 3 languages).

ai_tool.how_used: Generated business recommendations in English, Arabic, and Chinese for evaluation; no human received assistance in this study (p. 2, Methods).

task.description: Generate recommendations addressing hypothetical business issues in marketing, customer service, human resources, and R&D (p. 2, Methods).

studies.label: Study 2: randomized business-email writing; testing setting not stated

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual participants were randomly assigned to receive pre-generated GPT-4 content with the email-writing task or to write without AI-generated content. Language is a participant-group characteristic; the paper does not say that language was randomly assigned. The PDF does not identify a supervised lab, an online panel, or an ordinary workplace/coursework setting, so the randomized subtype is left unresolved under other (p. 2, Methods; p. 9, Limitations).
assignment.quote: The participants were randomly assigned to either a treatment group, wherein they were provided with AI-generated content to assist their writing of an email to address a hypothetical business issue;
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 3, Methods: https://osf.io/u7s2g; preregistration reported by the article, not independently retrieved.

arms.name: AI-generated content
arms.description: Supplied GPT-4 recommendations in the participant's language were displayed as text directly below the task instruction while the participant wrote the email; 240 participants are reported in this condition (p. 2, Research motivation and overview).

arms.name: No AI-generated content
arms.description: Participants wrote an email as in a typical work setting, without AI-generated assistance; 240 participants are reported in this condition (p. 2, Research motivation and overview; Methods).

participants.exclusions: The paper states: The sample includes all responses that passed the attention check and in which participants took more than the 15-minute suggested time (p. 3, Methods). It gives neither an initial assignment count nor the number excluded. The reported study sample of 480 and condition counts of 240 are coded as analyzed; their pre-exclusion assignment counts are left null. Exact participant flow needs the missing supplement.
participants.who: People proficient in English, Arabic, or Chinese; 160 per language in the reported study sample (pp. 1-2). Recruitment source, occupations, and whether they were online-panel participants are not stated in the main PDF; demographics are referred to SI Tables S3 and S4 (p. 2).
participants.country: Not stated; participants are described as spread across the world (p. 9, Limitations). Language groups are not treated as countries.
participants.quote: Specifically, a preregistered experiment was implemented, which involved 480 human participants (160 per language) proficient in English, Arabic, or Chinese.
participants.locator: p. 2, Research motivation and overview and Methods; p. 3, Methods, sample-inclusion sentence

ai_tool.how_used: Participants received pre-generated recommendations from Study 1 directly below their task instructions (p. 2, Research motivation and overview). They did not repeatedly interact with a live LLM; the paper describes this restriction in p. 9, Limitations. The supplied AI text was available while the scored email was produced.

task.description: Write an email proposing responses to a hypothetical business issue in marketing, customer service, human resources, or R&D. Creativity was judged on suggestions beyond the average manager's repertoire, so this is an output-rated creative problem-solving writing task (pp. 2-3, Methods).
task.duration: 15 minutes suggested; the included sample took more than that suggested time (p. 3, Methods).

outcomes.name: Email creativity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The creativity rating concerns multiple suggestions outside the creative repertoire of the average manager (p. 3, Methods). Six trained human evaluators rated the emails (p. 2, Methods). Figure 1 uses a 1-5 scale (pp. 4-5). The paper defines Y_i as the rating of email i and says all model standard errors were clustered at the participant level (p. 3, Statistical analysis). The main PDF does not establish whether individual evaluator ratings or averages of evaluator ratings constitute regression rows; unit and n_units are null pending SI Table S5. Study 2 evaluators are described as trained, but their professional qualifications are not specified in the main text, so the measure is coded human_raters. Prompt-length moderation checks are discussed with SI Tables S7 and S8 (pp. 4-5); these are variants of the same quality outcomes. Demographic/experience heterogeneity and alternative ordered-logit/control-variable analyses are summarized without estimates on p. 6, Task types (Study 2). Creativity is explicitly among the paper's primary outcomes (p. 3, Statistical analysis); the preregistration itself was not available for verification. Task-type variants remain in this outcome: p. 6, Task types (Study 2), reports less creative Chinese R&D emails relative to the marketing baseline (p = 0.025), citing SI Table S13; Fig. 3 (p. 8) displays R&D and non-R&D boxplots.

contrasts.reported: Figure 1(d) displays higher AI-treatment medians than control medians in English, Arabic, and Chinese. These are language-specific boxplots, not a pooled treatment-effect estimate. Numerical arm means, SDs, within-language AI-versus-control coefficients, and SEs are not printed in the main PDF.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Fig. 1(d); p. 3, Results, AI effects on the quality of human work across languages (Study 2), referring to SI Table S5

contrasts.treatment_arm: AI effect in Chinese (AI-generated content versus no AI-generated content)
contrasts.control_arm: AI effect in English (AI-generated content versus no AI-generated content)
contrasts.reported: AI treatment is associated with 0.49 standard deviations less Creativity in Chinese than in English (p = 0.016). This is the difference in treatment effects across languages; it is not the AI-versus-control effect within Chinese. No SE, confidence interval, or standardizing SD is given in the main PDF.
contrasts.locator: p. 3, Results, AI effects on the quality of human work across languages (Study 2); interaction specification (2); SI Table S5 referenced but absent

outcomes.name: Email actionability
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Actionability means clear solutions to a business issue and examples of action steps (p. 3, Methods). Six trained human evaluators rated the emails (p. 2, Methods). Figure 1 uses a 1-5 scale (pp. 4-5). The paper defines Y_i as the rating of email i and says all model standard errors were clustered at the participant level (p. 3, Statistical analysis). The main PDF does not establish whether individual evaluator ratings or averages of evaluator ratings constitute regression rows; unit and n_units are null pending SI Table S5. Study 2 evaluators are described as trained, but their professional qualifications are not specified in the main text, so the measure is coded human_raters. Prompt-length moderation checks are discussed with SI Tables S7 and S8 (pp. 4-5); these are variants of the same quality outcomes. Demographic/experience heterogeneity and alternative ordered-logit/control-variable analyses are summarized without estimates on p. 6, Task types (Study 2). This is one of the four named primary quality outcomes (p. 3, Statistical analysis). The task-type variant reports less actionable Arabic R&D emails relative to the marketing baseline (p = 0.053; p. 6, Task types, citing SI Table S13); Fig. 2 (p. 7) displays R&D and non-R&D boxplots.

contrasts.reported: Figure 1(c) shows higher AI-treatment medians in English and Chinese, while the Arabic median is unchanged. Numerical within-language AI-versus-control effects and their uncertainty are not printed; the available numerical results below compare treatment effects between languages.

outcomes.name: Email length (normalized characters)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Directly computed email length, measured as the number of normalized characters (p. 6, AI effects on productivity across languages, Study 2). The normalization procedure is not specified in the main PDF. The measure field is null because the vocabulary does not unambiguously describe a direct character count; no creativity-scoring model or lexical-overlap calculation is reported. Task-type variants are kept here: R&D emails were shorter in Arabic (p = 0.037) and Chinese (p = 0.020) relative to the marketing baseline (p. 6, Task types, citing SI Table S13). The p_value_only flags below indicate that no SE or interval is available; the raw changes and percentage changes are also printed and are retained verbatim.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No cross-paper reuse of participants is stated. Study 2 reuses AI-generated recommendations from Study 1; this is shared stimulus material, not evidence of a reused human participant sample.

eligibility.reason: Study 2 explicitly randomly assigns individual people to supplied GPT-4 recommendations versus no AI assistance (p. 2, Methods). The reported analysis sample is 480 people, including 240 per condition and 160 per language, rather than an idea or rating count (pp. 1-2; inclusion rule on p. 3). Creativity and other quality dimensions are rated on the emails that participants write with the assigned assistance available (pp. 2-3, Methods; pp. 4-5, Fig. 1). All three core criteria are met. The main PDF does not establish which of lab_rct, online_rct, or field_rct applies, so Study 2 uses other with randomization explicitly recorded. Study 1 is model_only and independently does not qualify.

one_line_finding: In the reported 480-person email-writing experiment, the AI effect on creativity was 0.49 standard deviations smaller in Chinese than in English (p = 0.016; p. 2, Methods, for the count; p. 3, Results, Study 2, for the contrast).
open_questions: Retrieve the separate SI, especially Section A and Tables S3-S5, to confirm the testing setting/recruitment source, initial randomized sample, exclusions, and per-language condition counts; these details are not stated in the main PDF.

SI Table S5 is needed to establish whether the quality regressions use individual ratings or evaluator-averaged email scores as rows and to obtain numerical within-language AI-versus-control effects, arm descriptives, standard errors, and the denominator of the reported standard-deviation units.
Confirm the evaluator qualifications for Study 2 and the character-normalization procedure in the SI; the main PDF does not supply them.
The outcome-measure vocabulary has no exact direct-character-count category; email-length measure is left null rather than labeling it lexical overlap or a creativity-scoring model.
Check the OSF preregistration before distinguishing preregistered primary outcomes from the four primary dimensions explicitly named in the article.
notes: Read all 10 PDF pages and the entire markdown conversion (306 lines). Inspected all main-text figures before the design and methods: Fig. 1(a-d), pp. 4-5, reports completeness, relevance, actionability, and creativity; Fig. 2, p. 7, repeats actionability by task type; Fig. 3, p. 8, repeats creativity by task type. No appendix or SI is appended to this PDF. Full outcome inventory: Study 1 reports completeness, relevance, actionability, and creativity of model-generated responses (p. 3, Study 1 Results; SI Figs. S2-S3 and Tables S1-S2). These model-only results answer none of the three human-assistance questions and are inventoried here rather than added as eligible outcome entries. Study 2 reports the four email-quality dimensions, email length, writing time, self-reported confidence, and perceived difficulty (pp. 3-6). The five output-scored Study 2 outcomes are entered; writing time is a process measure, and confidence/difficulty are self-reports, so those three are not entered. No diversity or post-removal outcome is reported. Task-type and robustness variants are retained within their parent outcomes. Language-by-treatment differences are explicitly labeled as other contrasts between AI effects, not as a Chinese/Arabic AI-versus-control effect or an ai_design experiment. Numbers printed as p = 0.000 are retained exactly; no effect sizes, standard errors, means, or counts were calculated from the figures. The reported 480 is treated as the analyzed study sample in light of the inclusion rule, with the assignment denominator left unresolved. Unknown population, quality-analysis unit, and the unmatched email-length measure use null. Data URL is from p. 9, Data availability; no code URL is provided. Attempts to inspect the supplementary source via Python urllib with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 at the named PMC S3 source and Nature article both failed with a socket-permission error; nothing was downloaded or saved. Only this screening JSON is written.
